A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same NFIG research work. Their complete text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: v2 reports original ImageNet generation and reconstruction results, component ablations, generated examples and frequency-guidance analyses in Section 4.

after.justification: v4 retains those original results and adds model-scaling, training-duration, frequency-preservation, cross-domain reconstruction and failure-case results.

M1.justification: The FFT decomposition, frequency-guided residual quantization, frequency-band schedule and autoregressive prediction procedure remain unchanged. Appendix B.1 newly documents losses, and Section 4.1 clarifies implementation provenance; neither establishes a revised method.

E1.justification: Appendix B.4 extends FR-VAE reconstruction evaluation beyond ImageNet to DTD, QRCODE, Diagrams, Chest-X, CelebA-HQ, COCO and LSUN-Bedroom. This substantially broadens image-domain coverage. These additions concern reconstruction; class-conditional generation remains evaluated on ImageNet-256.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds three FAR configurations at 208M, 427M and 812M parameters, plus XQGAN-310M, while retaining the previous comparators. FAR and XQGAN were already discussed in v2 but lacked these reported comparisons. Their inclusion substantively expands evaluation against closely related frequency-based and tokenizer approaches.

E3.justification: v4 adds a controlled 55-epoch comparison of 310M and 600M models, a 200–350-epoch training series with VAR training-budget comparisons, and PSD/FKS frequency evaluation with specified band weights. These materially expand the evaluation design; the original 350-epoch NFIG configuration remains unchanged.

E4.justification: New analyses examine model-size scaling, training-duration sensitivity, frequency preservation against VAR-16, and anatomical, texture and detail failures. The original component ablation is retained as Table 5, formerly Table 3, and the quantization-loss comparison remains. Figure 4 also replaces its progressive reconstruction example.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests for its experimental results. The additional results retain point-estimate reporting.

E6.justification: Existing Table 2 scores, including NFIG rFID 0.85 and gFID 2.81, remain unchanged. New results include 55-epoch FIDs of 5.47 and 5.07 for 310M and 600M models, and 310M FIDs of 3.35, 3.16 and 2.93 at 200, 250 and 300 epochs. Appendix B adds FKS scores of 87.6% versus VAR-16's 79.5%, reconstruction scores and failure findings. These are additional results, not improvements over matched v2 runs.

T1.justification: Appendix B.1 adds explicit mathematical specifications of the tokenizer objective and transformer loss in Eqs. 10–11. Existing Eqs. 1–9 and Appendix A's Fourier mathematics remain unchanged. No theorem or proof is added; the removed quantum-field appendix was a conceptual analogy.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contributions and conclusion retain the same central claims: frequency-ordered autoregressive generation, the FR-VAE tokenizer, reconstruction FID 0.85, generation FID 2.81 and the speed advantage over VAR-d20. New experiments support these retained claims.

C2.justification: v4 adds an argument that the XQGAN comparison attributes benefits beyond tokenizer quality to frequency priors, and interprets observed failures as difficulties maintaining semantic consistency across frequency bands. It removes the quantum-field analogy and expands future directions toward beneficial noise, multimodal alignment and privacy, substantially revising the explanatory and limitations discussion.

D1.justification: v4 adds a project-code access link, identifies XQGAN's tokenizer implementation strategy, and documents reconstruction, perceptual, GAN and cross-entropy losses, including the GAN weight of 0.5. Most existing hardware and hyperparameters are retained. Equation 10's identical feature terms leave part of the new loss specification unclear.

R1.justification: The existing related-work discussion is largely retained. Six references, 43–48, add connections to beneficial noise, augmentation, vision-language alignment and adversarial privacy, mainly in future work. The clarified relationship to XQGAN also refines implementation and contribution positioning.

P1.justification: The main section order and most prose remain intact. Local revisions expand the results discussion, rewrite parts of the limitations section, update affiliations and contact information, and replace the conceptual Appendix B with experimental and technical subsections and corresponding cross-references.

P2.justification: v4 substantially expands the evidence displays with two new main-text tables, two appendix tables and an annotated failure-case figure. Table 2 gains comparator rows, Figure 4 replaces its image/spectrum sequence and updates its attribution, and the retained ablation table and other displays are repositioned.

improvement.justification: Table 4 improves comparison fairness by reporting equal-size, 200-epoch results: NFIG FID 3.35 versus VAR-d16's 3.55. Added frequency measurements, failure cases and implementation disclosures improve support and transparency beyond v2. The gains are limited by underspecified appendix metrics and dataset protocols, plus Equation 10's feature-minus-itself term. Overall, the evidence is stronger, while the method and headline results remain unchanged.
